item.title: Getting Started
item.description:
Getting Started

Runnable examples covering the main ways to embed rust-meth-lib in your own tooling. Each file is self-contained and documents its own [dependencies] snippet.

basic_query.rs

This example first locates the rust-analyzer binary, then it queries the available methods on a RefCell<u8> and prints the results.

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::{find_rust_analyzer, query_methods};

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;

    let methods = query_methods("RefCell<u8>", &ra_path, None)?;

    println!("Methods on RefCell<u8> ({} total):", methods.len());
    for method in &methods {
        println!("  {}", method.name);
    }

    Ok(())
}

Output

The minimal end-to-end path: find_rust_analyzer → query_methods → print method names.

Methods on RefCell<u8> (30 total):
  as_ptr
  borrow
  borrow_mut
  clamp
  clone
  clone_from
  clone_into
  cmp
  eq
  ge
  get_mut
  gt
  into
  into_inner
  le
  lt
  max
  min
  ne
  partial_cmp
  replace
  replace_with
  swap
  take
  to_owned
  try_borrow
  try_borrow_mut
  try_borrow_unguarded
  try_into
  undo_leak

Limit Number of Methods Returned from Standard API

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::{Method, find_rust_analyzer, query_methods};

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    // Step 1: locate the rust-analyzer binary.
    //
    // find_rust_analyzer checks `PATH` first, then falls back to the rustup
    // component directory (~/.rustup/toolchains/<active>/bin/rust-analyzer).
    // Returns `RustMethError::RustAnalyzerNotFound` if neither exists.
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;

    // Step 2: query methods.
    //
    // query_methods spins up an ephemeral LSP session, synthesises a
    // temporary Cargo project with `let _x: RefCell<u8> = todo!();`, triggers
    // a completion request at the dot position, and tears everything down.
    //
    // The third argument is `deps: Option<&str>`: `None` means stdlib only.
    let methods = query_methods("RefCell<u8>", &ra_path, None)?;

    let top5: Vec<Method> = methods.into_iter().take(5).collect();

    // println!("Methods on RefCell<u8> ({} total):", methods.len());
    println!("First 5 methods on RefCell<u8>:");
    // for method in &methods {
    for method in &top5 {
        println!("  {}", method.name);
    }

    Ok(())
}

Output

First 5 methods on RefCell<u8>:
  as_ptr
  borrow
  borrow_mut
  clamp
  clone

Using the Builder API

The same query using [MethodQuery], equivalent to the above but chainable:

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::find_rust_analyzer;
use rust_meth_lib::query::MethodQuery;

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;
    let methods = MethodQuery::new("RefCell<u8>")
        .run(&ra_path)?;

    println!("Methods on RefCell<u8> ({} total):", methods.len());
    for method in &methods {
        println!("  {}", method.name);
    }
    Ok(())
}

The builder becomes more useful when combining options, adding a filter or resolving source locations without separate function calls:

let methods = MethodQuery::new("RefCell<u8>")
    .filter("borrow")
    .run(&ra_path)?;

With the filter above, the output is (I changed the print statement to match):

Methods on RefCell<u8> with borrow in their name (5 total):
  borrow
  borrow_mut
  try_borrow
  try_borrow_mut
  try_borrow_unguarded

Limit the Number of Methods Returned

You can use the .limit() method to return N methods. For example, a Vec<u8>, returns over 200 methods. To only return the first 10 sorted alphabetically:

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::find_rust_analyzer;
use rust_meth_lib::query::MethodQuery;

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;
    let methods = MethodQuery::new("Vec<u8>").limit(10).run(&ra_path)?;

    println!("First 10 methods on Vec<u8>:");
    for method in &methods {
        println!("  {}", method.name);
    }
    Ok(())
}

Output

First 10 methods on Vec<u8>:
  align_to
  align_to_mut
  allocator
  append
  array_windows
  as_array
  as_ascii
  as_ascii_unchecked
  as_chunks
  as_chunks_mut

item.title: rust-meth-lib
item.description:
rust-meth-lib

Core library powering rust-meth. Discovers methods available on any Rust type by driving a rust-analyzer LSP session.

Overview

rust-meth-lib provides the building blocks for programmatically querying rust-analyzer:

  • Spinning up and managing an LSP session (LspTransport)
  • Synthesizing a temporary Rust project and injecting the target type (Probe)
  • Requesting completions and go-to-definition results from rust-analyzer
  • Fuzzy-filtering and ranking method results
  • Exposing utilities for embedding rust-meth workflows in other tools
  • Full working Examples

Please file an Issue if any problems arise.

Workspace layout

rust-meth/
├── Cargo.toml               — workspace manifest
├── lib/                     — rust-meth-lib (this crate)
│   ├── Cargo.toml
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── benches/
│   │   └── benchmarks.rs
│   └── src/
│       ├── lib.rs
│       ├── error.rs
│       ├── lsp.rs
│       ├── probe.rs
│       └── analyzer/
│           ├── mod.rs
│           ├── discovery.rs
│           ├── parse.rs
│           └── session.rs
└── cli/                     : standalone binary crate that calls into this library
    ├── Cargo.toml
    └── src/
        └── main.rs

UI components, CLI argument parsing, interactive selection, and spinner display are now maintained in cli/.

Public API

Key Types

ItemDescription
LspTransportManages the stdio JSON-RPC channel to a rust-analyzer process
ProbeBuilds a temporary Cargo project that makes the target type available for LSP queries
analyzerHigh-level session orchestrator, combines Probe + LspTransport to return method completions

Basic Usage

[dependencies]
rust-meth-lib = "0.3.0"
  • rust_meth_lib docs.rs

Full working Example:

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::{find_rust_analyzer, query_methods};

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;
    let methods = query_methods("Result<u8, &'static str>", &ra_path, None)?;

    println!("Methods available for Result<u8, &'static str>");
    for method in &methods {
        println!("{}", method.name);
    }

    Ok(())
}

The exact list returned varies by toolchain.

The primary APIs are intended for embedding or extending the rust-meth workflow.
The CLI interface is maintained in a separate crate.

Builder API

MethodQuery provides a chainable interface over query_methods and filter_methods. Use .filter() to narrow results by match quality (exact > prefix > substring), and .run_with_definitions() to also resolve source locations.

// Query + filter
MethodQuery::new("String")
    .filter("push")
    .run(&ra_path)?;

// Query + filter + source locations
MethodQuery::new("serde_json::Value")
    .deps(r#"serde_json = "1.0""#)
    .filter("as_str")
    .run_with_definitions(&ra_path)?;

See builder_run.rs and builder_definitions.rs for full examples.

Error Handling

The library uses a single RustMethError enum (via thiserror) and a Result<T> alias over it:

pub type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, RustMethError>;
VariantCause
IoOS / file system errors (std::io::Error)
JsonJSON serialization or deserialization failure
ParseIntString-to-integer conversion failure
NoContentLengthLSP response missing a Content-Length header
RecvExhausted { limit }Message loop hit limit without matching a response
UnexpectedResponseShapeStructurally valid JSON but missing expected fields
RustAnalyzerNotFoundrust-analyzer not on PATH or in component directory
MissingStdinstdin handle wasn’t captured
MissingStdoutstdout handle wasn’t captured
TypeNotFoundrust-analyzer diagnostic error for the probed type
Timeoutrust-analyzer failed to produce a usable response within retry budget
FeatureGatedType exists but requires a feature flag that wasn’t enabled for this probe

All fallible functions in this crate return rust_meth_lib::Result<T>. If you’re embedding the library, you can convert into your own error type via ? since RustMethError implements std::error::Error.

use rust_meth_lib::{Result, analyzer::{find_rust_analyzer, query_methods}};

fn my_wrapper() -> Result<()> {
    // RustAnalyzerNotFound, Io, Json, etc. all propagate with ?
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;
    let _methods = query_methods("Vec<u8>", &ra_path, None)?;
    Ok(())
}

rust-meth-lib examples

Runnable examples covering the main ways to embed rust-meth-lib in your own tooling. Each file is self-contained and documents its own [dependencies] snippet.

Running the Examples

To run the examples locally, clone the repo:

git clone https://github.com/saylesss88/rust-meth.git
cd rust-meth/lib
cargo run --example basic_query

The examples require rust-analyzer on your PATH:

rustup component add rust-analyzer

cargo run --example basic_query
cargo run --example method_info
cargo run --example third_party_crate   # slow on first run (downloads serde_json)
cargo run --example fuzzy_filter
cargo run --example go_to_definition
cargo run --example custom_error
cargo run --example batch_query

Examples start at Getting Started

item.title: Querying Methods
item.description:
Querying Methods

Shows how to work with the richer fields on [Method] beyond just the name:

  • Method::detail: the full function signature as a string (e.g. "const fn(&self) -> *mut T"), returned by rust-analyzer as the completion item’s detail field. Option<String>: not always present, especially for trait-provided methods on generic types.
  • Method::documentation: the rustdoc string for the method, often multi-line. Option<String>: coverage varies by crate and method.

Both fields are None when rust-analyzer doesn’t return them. Methods with neither still appear in the results from query_methods. This example filters to only those with at least one field populated, and renders them gracefully when the other is absent.

method_info.rs

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::{Method, find_rust_analyzer, query_methods};

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;

    let methods = query_methods("Cell<u8>", &ra_path, None)?;

    // Only print methods that have at least a signature. Methods with
    // neither detail nor docs still exist in the list, they're just
    // less useful for display purposes.
    let documented: Vec<&Method> = methods
        .iter()
        .filter(|m| m.detail.is_some() || m.documentation.is_some())
        .collect();

    println!(
        "{} of {} Cell<u8> methods have signatures or docs:\n",
        documented.len(),
        methods.len()
    );

    for method in documented {
        // The signature line (e.g. "pub fn push_str(&mut self, string: &str)")
        if let Some(sig) = &method.detail {
            println!("fn {}  →  {sig}", method.name);
        } else {
            println!("fn {} (no signature)", method.name);
        }

        // Rustdoc
        if let Some(doc) = &method.documentation {
            // Just the first sentence to keep output manageable.
            let first_line = doc.lines().next().unwrap_or("").trim();
            if !first_line.is_empty() {
                println!("  doc: {first_line}");
            }
        }

        println!();
    }

    Ok(())
}

Output

26 of 26 Cell<u8> methods have signatures or docs:

fn as_ptr  →  const fn(&self) -> *mut T
  doc: Returns a raw pointer to the underlying data in this cell.

fn clamp  →  fn(self, Self, Self) -> Self
  doc: Restrict a value to a certain interval.

fn clone  →  fn(&self) -> Self
  doc: Returns a duplicate of the value.

fn clone_from  →  fn(&mut self, &Self)
  doc: Performs copy-assignment from `source`.

fn clone_into  →  fn(&self, &mut <Self as ToOwned>::Owned)
  doc: Uses borrowed data to replace owned data, usually by cloning.

fn cmp  →  fn(&self, &Self) -> Ordering
  doc: This method returns an [`Ordering`] between `self` and `other`.

fn eq  →  fn(&self, &Rhs) -> bool
  doc: Equality operator `==`.

fn ge  →  fn(&self, &Rhs) -> bool
  doc: Tests greater than or equal to (for `self` and `other`) and is used by

fn get  →  const fn(&self) -> T
  doc: Returns a copy of the contained value.

fn get_mut  →  const fn(&mut self) -> &mut T
  doc: Returns a mutable reference to the underlying data.

fn gt  →  fn(&self, &Rhs) -> bool
  doc: Tests greater than (for `self` and `other`) and is used by the `>`

fn into  →  fn(self) -> T
  doc: Converts this type into the (usually inferred) input type.

fn into_inner  →  const fn(self) -> T
  doc: Unwraps the value, consuming the cell.

fn le  →  fn(&self, &Rhs) -> bool
  doc: Tests less than or equal to (for `self` and `other`) and is used by the

fn lt  →  fn(&self, &Rhs) -> bool
  doc: Tests less than (for `self` and `other`) and is used by the `<` operator.

fn max  →  fn(self, Self) -> Self
  doc: Compares and returns the maximum of two values.

fn min  →  fn(self, Self) -> Self
  doc: Compares and returns the minimum of two values.

fn ne  →  fn(&self, &Rhs) -> bool
  doc: Inequality operator `!=`.

fn partial_cmp  →  fn(&self, &Rhs) -> Option<Ordering>
  doc: This method returns an ordering between `self` and `other` values if one exists.

fn replace  →  const fn(&self, T) -> T
  doc: Replaces the contained value with `val`, and returns the old contained value.

fn set  →  const fn(&self, T)
  doc: Sets the contained value.

fn swap  →  fn(&self, &Cell<T>)
  doc: Swaps the values of two `Cell`s.

fn take  →  const fn(&self) -> T
  doc: Takes the value of the cell, leaving `Default::default()` in its place.

fn to_owned  →  fn(&self) -> <Self as ToOwned>::Owned
  doc: Creates owned data from borrowed data, usually by cloning.

fn try_into  →  fn(self) -> Result<T, <Self as TryInto<T>>::Error>
  doc: Performs the conversion.

fn update  →  const fn(&self, impl FnOnce(T) -> T)
  doc: Updates the contained value using a function.

item.title: Batch Query
item.description:
Batch Query

Querying multiple types and aggregating the results.

query_methods_batch runs each query in parallel: one thread per type, each with its own independent rust-analyzer subprocess. Total wall time is roughly the cost of the slowest single query rather than the sum of all. Errors are per-type and do not abort the batch.

batch_query.rs

For Vec<u8>, VecDeque<u8>, and LinkedList<u8>, this example returns:

  • Per-type method counts: printed after all queries complete
  • Common methods: the intersection across all three types
  • Unique methods: what each type has that neither of the others does
use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::{find_rust_analyzer, query_methods_batch};
use rust_meth_lib::error::RustMethError;
use std::collections::{BTreeMap, BTreeSet};

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;

    let queries: &[(&str, Option<&str>)] = &[
        ("Vec<u8>", None),
        ("VecDeque<u8>", None),
        ("LinkedList<u8>", None),
    ];

    // All three queries run in parallel. Results come back in input order.
    let batch_results = query_methods_batch(queries, &ra_path);

    // -- Partition into successes and failures --

    let mut results: BTreeMap<&str, BTreeSet<String>> = BTreeMap::new();
    let mut failures: Vec<(&str, RustMethError)> = Vec::new();

    for (type_name, result) in batch_results {
        match result {
            Ok(methods) => {
                let names: BTreeSet<String> = methods.into_iter().map(|m| m.name).collect();
                println!("{type_name}: {} methods", names.len());
                results.insert(type_name, names);
            }
            Err(e) => {
                eprintln!("{type_name}: FAILED: {e}");
                failures.push((type_name, e));
            }
        }
    }

    println!();

    // -- Methods common to all successfully queried types --

    if results.len() >= 2 {
        let mut common = results.values().next().cloned().unwrap_or_default();
        for set in results.values().skip(1) {
            common = common.intersection(set).cloned().collect();
        }

        println!(
            "Methods common to all {} types ({} total):",
            results.len(),
            common.len()
        );
        for name in &common {
            println!("  {name}");
        }
        println!();
    }

    // -- Per-type unique methods --
    //
    // What does each type have that none of the others do?

    for (type_name, methods) in &results {
        let others_union: BTreeSet<&String> = results
            .iter()
            .filter(|(t, _)| *t != type_name)
            .flat_map(|(_, s)| s.iter())
            .collect();

        let unique: Vec<&String> = methods
            .iter()
            .filter(|m| !others_union.contains(m))
            .collect();

        if unique.is_empty() {
            println!("{type_name}: no unique methods");
        } else {
            println!("{type_name} unique methods ({}):", unique.len());
            for name in unique {
                println!("  {name}");
            }
        }
        println!();
    }

    // -- Summary of failures --

    if !failures.is_empty() {
        println!("Failed queries:");
        for (type_name, err) in failures {
            println!("  {type_name}: {err}");
        }
    }

    Ok(())
}

item.title: Error Handling
item.description:
Error Handling

All fallible functions in rust-meth-lib return rust_meth_lib::Result<T>, a type alias over a single [RustMethError] enum. This makes it easy to propagate errors with ? in your own code, and to convert them into your application’s own error type when you need custom messages or behaviour.

RustMethError variants

VariantCause
RustAnalyzerNotFoundrust-analyzer not on PATH or in rustup component directory
TypeNotFoundThe probed type doesn’t exist or isn’t in scope
FeatureGatedType exists but requires a feature flag not enabled in the probe
Timeoutrust-analyzer failed to respond within the retry budget
IoOS or filesystem error
JsonJSON serialization or deserialization failure
UnexpectedResponseShapeStructurally valid JSON but missing expected fields
RecvExhaustedMessage loop hit its limit without matching a response

Custom error types

The most common embedding pattern is wrapping RustMethError in your own thiserror enum. Since RustMethError implements std::error::Error, it converts with ? directly, but a manual From impl lets you intercept specific variants for custom messages before falling through to a generic wrapper for everything else.

The example below intercepts RustAnalyzerNotFound and TypeNotFound to give actionable error messages, while passing everything else through as a generic QueryFailed.

custom_error.rs

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::{find_rust_analyzer, query_methods};
use rust_meth_lib::error::RustMethError;

// -- Your application's error type --

#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
enum AppError {
    /// rust-analyzer isn't installed, give a helpful message.
    #[error("rust-analyzer not found. Install it with: rustup component add rust-analyzer")]
    RustAnalyzerMissing,

    /// The type the user asked about doesn't exist.
    #[error(
        "Unknown type `{type_name}`. Check the spelling and that any required crate is listed in deps."
    )]
    UnknownType { type_name: String },

    /// Anything else from the library becomes a generic query failure.
    #[error("LSP query failed: {0}")]
    QueryFailed(RustMethError),
}

// -- Conversion --
//
// We can't use `#[from]` for everything because we want to intercept specific
// variants. Instead, write a manual `From` impl that matches the cases we care
// about and falls through to the generic wrapper for everything else.

impl From<RustMethError> for AppError {
    fn from(err: RustMethError) -> Self {
        match err {
            RustMethError::RustAnalyzerNotFound => Self::RustAnalyzerMissing,
            RustMethError::TypeNotFound { type_name, .. } => Self::UnknownType { type_name },
            other => Self::QueryFailed(other),
        }
    }
}

// -- Application logic --

fn lookup(type_name: &str) -> Result<(), AppError> {
    // find_rust_analyzer() returns RustMethError::RustAnalyzerNotFound on
    // failure, which our From impl converts to AppError::RustAnalyzerMissing.
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;

    // query_methods() returns RustMethError::TypeNotFound for bad type names,
    // which our From impl converts to AppError::UnknownType.
    let methods = query_methods(type_name, &ra_path, None)?;

    println!("{type_name}: {} methods", methods.len());
    for m in methods.iter().take(5) {
        println!("  {}", m.name);
    }
    if methods.len() > 5 {
        println!("  ...and {} more", methods.len() - 5);
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    // Use a type that will succeed.
    match lookup("Vec<u8>") {
        Ok(()) => {}
        Err(e) => eprintln!("error: {e}"),
    }

    println!();

    // Use a type that will fail with `TypeNotFound`, demonstrates the
    // custom error message path.
    match lookup("NonExistentType") {
        Ok(()) => {}
        Err(AppError::UnknownType { type_name }) => {
            eprintln!("Type not found: `{type_name}`");
            eprintln!("Tip: check spelling, or pass deps for third-party crates.");
        }
        Err(e) => eprintln!("error: {e}"),
    }
}

Output

Vec<u8>: 229 methods
  align_to
  align_to_mut
  allocator
  append
  array_windows
  ...and 224 more

Type not found: `NonExistentType`
Tip: check spelling, or pass deps for third-party crates.

item.title: Filtering
item.description:
Filtering

Filters and ranks methods against a query string without re-querying rust-analyzer. Useful if you already have a Vec<Method> and want to narrow results. Exact matches score highest, then prefix, then substring. Non-matching methods are excluded entirely.

filter_methods.rs

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::{find_rust_analyzer, query_methods};
use rust_meth_lib::query::filter_methods;

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;
    let methods = query_methods("HashMap<String, u32>", &ra_path, None)?;
    let filtered = filter_methods(&methods, "get");
    println!("HashMap<String, u32> methods matching \"get\":\n");
    for m in filtered {
        println!("{}", m.name);
    }
    Ok(())
}

Output

HashMap<String, u32> methods matching "get":

get
get_disjoint_mut
get_disjoint_unchecked_mut
get_key_value
get_mut

fuzzy_filter.rs

query_methods returns a plain Vec<Method>: already sorted and deduplicated, ready to filter however you like. This example shows a few patterns: substring match, signature grep, and a simple ranked scorer. If you’re building a TUI or editor plugin on top of the library, this is the pattern to follow.

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::{Method, find_rust_analyzer, query_methods};

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;
    let methods = query_methods("HashMap<String, u32>", &ra_path, None)?;

    let query = "get";

    println!("All methods containing \"{query}\":");
    println!("{}", "-".repeat(40));

    // -- 1. Simple substring filter --
    let matched: Vec<&Method> = methods.iter().filter(|m| m.name.contains(query)).collect();

    for m in &matched {
        println!("  {}", m.name);
    }

    println!();

    // -- 2. Signature grep --
    //
    // Filter on the `detail` field to find methods with a specific return type.
    // Useful when you want to narrow results by type, not just name.

    let returns_option: Vec<&Method> = methods
        .iter()
        .filter(|m| {
            m.detail
                .as_deref()
                .is_some_and(|sig| sig.contains("-> Option"))
        })
        .collect();

    println!("Methods returning Option<_>:");
    println!("{}", "-".repeat(40));
    for m in &returns_option {
        println!(
            "  {}  →  {}",
            m.name,
            m.detail.as_deref().unwrap_or("(no signature)")
        );
    }

    println!();

    // -- 3. Simple ranked scorer --
    //
    // Score each method by how closely it matches the query: prefix match
    // scores higher than substring match, exact match highest. This gives
    // you a starting point for building fuzzy ranking without pulling in
    // a whole fuzzy-matching crate.

    println!("Ranked results for \"{query}\":");
    println!("{}", "-".repeat(40));

    let mut scored: Vec<(u8, &Method)> = methods
        .iter()
        .filter_map(|m| {
            let score = if m.name == query {
                3 // exact
            } else if m.name.starts_with(query) {
                2 // prefix
            } else if m.name.contains(query) {
                1 // substring
            } else {
                return None;
            };
            Some((score, m))
        })
        .collect();

    // Sort descending by score; stable within each tier (already alpha-sorted
    // from query_methods).
    scored.sort_by_key(|item| std::cmp::Reverse(item.0));

    for (score, m) in scored {
        let label = match score {
            3 => "exact ",
            2 => "prefix",
            _ => "substr",
        };
        println!("  [{label}]  {}", m.name);
    }

    Ok(())
}

Output

All methods containing "get":
----------------------------------------
  get
  get_disjoint_mut
  get_disjoint_unchecked_mut
  get_key_value
  get_mut

Methods returning Option<_>:
----------------------------------------
  get  →  fn(&self, &Q) -> Option<&V>
  get_key_value  →  fn(&self, &Q) -> Option<(&K, &V)>
  get_mut  →  fn(&mut self, &Q) -> Option<&mut V>
  insert  →  fn(&mut self, K, V) -> Option<V>
  remove  →  fn(&mut self, &Q) -> Option<V>
  remove_entry  →  fn(&mut self, &Q) -> Option<(K, V)>

Ranked results for "get":
----------------------------------------
  [exact ]  get
  [prefix]  get_disjoint_mut
  [prefix]  get_disjoint_unchecked_mut
  [prefix]  get_key_value
  [prefix]  get_mut

item.title: Definitions
item.description:
Definitions

This chapter covers how to locate the actual source code definitions for methods across standard library and third-party types using rust-analyzer.

go_to_definition.rs

  1. Direct Definition Queries

The go_to_definition.rs example demonstrates how to query a specific type and method combination to find its absolute and relative paths on disk, alongside the line number.

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::{find_rust_analyzer, query_definition};

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;

    // -- Stdlib method --

    print_definition("Vec<u8>", "push", &ra_path, None)?;
    print_definition("String", "push_str", &ra_path, None)?;
    print_definition("HashMap<String, u32>", "insert", &ra_path, None)?;

    // -- Third-party method --

    let serde_deps = r#"serde_json = "1.0""#;
    print_definition("serde_json::Value", "as_str", &ra_path, Some(serde_deps))?;

    Ok(())
}

fn print_definition(
    type_name: &str,
    method_name: &str,
    ra_path: &std::path::Path,
    deps: Option<&str>,
) -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    print!("{type_name}::{method_name}  →  ");

    match query_definition(type_name, method_name, ra_path, deps)? {
        Some(def) => {
            // `path` is the display-friendly shortened form:
            //   "library/core/src/num/uint_macros.rs"
            //
            // `full_path` is the absolute path on disk, useful if you want
            // to open the file programmatically.
            //
            // `line` is 0-indexed (LSP convention). Add 1 for display.
            println!("{}:{}", def.path, def.line + 1);
            println!("       full: {}", def.full_path);
        }
        None => {
            // Not an error, `rust-analyzer` just doesn't have a source
            // location for this method. Common for compiler intrinsics.
            println!("(no source location found)");
        }
    }

    println!();
    Ok(())
}

Output

Vec<u8>::push  →  library/alloc/src/vec/mod.rs:995
       full: /home/jr/.rustup/toolchains/nightly-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/alloc/src/vec/mod.rs

String::push_str  →  library/alloc/src/string.rs:1104
       full: /home/jr/.rustup/toolchains/nightly-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/alloc/src/string.rs

HashMap<String, u32>::insert  →  library/std/src/collections/hash/map.rs:1332
       full: /home/jr/.rustup/toolchains/nightly-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/std/src/collections/hash/map.rs

serde_json::Value::as_str  →  src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/serde_json-1.0.151/src/value/mod.rs:492
       full: /home/jr/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/serde_json-1.0.151/src/value/mod.rs

builder_definitions.rs

  1. Builder Pattern with Definitions

The builder_definitions.rs example integrates definition lookup into the MethodQuery builder. This allows you to filter methods and immediately retrieve their source locations in a single workflow.

For third-party types, each matching method runs a separate definition query. Use a tight filter (exact or short prefix) to limit the number of queries. Results are not cached by the results cache since definition queries return source locations rather than method lists, expect similar times on every run for third-party types.

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::find_rust_analyzer;
use rust_meth_lib::query::MethodQuery;

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;

    // -- Stdlib type -- fast --

    let results = MethodQuery::new("Vec<u8>")
        .filter("drain")
        .run_with_definitions(&ra_path)?;

    println!("Vec<u8> methods matching \"drain\" with source locations:");
    for r in &results {
        match &r.definition {
            Some(def) => println!("  {}  →  {}:{}", r.method.name, def.path, def.line + 1),
            None => println!("  {}  →  (no source location)", r.method.name),
        }
    }

    println!();

    // -- Third-party type -- use an exact filter to limit definition queries.
    // Definition results are not cached, so this will always spin up
    // rust-analyzer. A broad filter like "as_" would multiply this cost
    // by the number of matches.

    println!("Querying serde_json::Value::as_str (may be slow on first run)...");
    let results = MethodQuery::new("serde_json::Value")
        .deps(r#"serde_json = "1.0""#)
        .filter("as_str")
        .run_with_definitions(&ra_path)?;

    println!("serde_json::Value methods matching \"as_str\" with source locations:");
    for r in &results {
        match &r.definition {
            Some(def) => println!("  {}  →  {}:{}", r.method.name, def.path, def.line + 1),
            None => println!("  {}  →  (no source location)", r.method.name),
        }
    }

    Ok(())
}

Output

Vec<u8> methods matching "drain" with source locations:
  drain  →  library/alloc/src/vec/mod.rs:3022

Querying serde_json::Value::as_str (may be slow on first run)...
serde_json::Value methods matching "as_str" with source locations:
  as_str  →  src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/serde_json-1.0.151/src/value/mod.rs:492

item.title: Builder API
item.description:
Builder API

Builder options

MethodDescription
MethodQuery::new(type_name)Start a query for the given type
.deps(toml)TOML dependency string for third-party crates
.filter(query)Narrow results by name (exact > prefix > substring)
.run(&ra_path)Execute and return Vec<Method>

builder_run.rs

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::find_rust_analyzer;

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;

    let methods = MethodQuery::new("String").filter("push").run(&ra_path)?;

    println!("String methods matching \"push\":");
    for m in &methods {

item.title: Results Cache
item.description:
Results Cache

The results_cache example demonstrates the caching mechanism introduced in version 0.4.0.

When querying methods for a type, the library normally spins up a rust-analyzer LSP session, which can take a few seconds. The results cache stores these outputs as JSON in $XDG_CACHE_HOME/rust-meth/results/. Subsequent calls, even across separate process runs, retrieve the data instantly with zero LSP overhead.

results_cache.rs

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::{find_rust_analyzer, query_methods};
use rust_meth_lib::results_cache::results_cache_entries;
use std::time::Instant;

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;

    // Uncomment to clear the cache on every run
    // rust_meth_lib::results_cache::clear_results_cache().ok();

    // -- First call -- cold results cache --
    println!("First call (cold cache)...");
    let t1 = Instant::now();
    let methods = query_methods("Vec<u8>", &ra_path, None)?;
    let elapsed1 = t1.elapsed();

    println!("  {} methods found in {:.2?}\n", methods.len(), elapsed1);

    // Inspect what was saved
    let entries = results_cache_entries();
    println!("Results cache now has {} entry:", entries.len());
    for e in &entries {
        println!(
            "  {} : {} methods (ra: {})",
            e.type_name, e.method_count, e.ra_version
        );
    }
    println!();

    // -- Second call -- results cache hit --
    println!("Second call (warm cache)...");
    let t2 = Instant::now();
    let methods2 = query_methods("Vec<u8>", &ra_path, None)?;
    let elapsed2 = t2.elapsed();

    println!("  {} methods found in {:.2?}\n", methods2.len(), elapsed2);

    // Summary
    let speedup = elapsed1.as_secs_f64() / elapsed2.as_secs_f64();
    println!("Speedup: {speedup:.0}x faster on cache hit");
    println!("\nRun this example again to see the persistent cache kick in");
    println!(
        "on the very first call (~0ms instead of ~{}s).",
        elapsed1.as_secs()
    );

    Ok(())
}

Output

First call (cold cache)...
  229 methods found in 3.66s

Results cache now has 1 entry:
  Vec<u8> : 229 methods (ra: rust-analyzer 1.100.0-nightly (34baba5 2026-08-16))

Second call (warm cache)...
  229 methods found in 17.29ms

Speedup: 212x faster on cache hit

Run this example again to see the persistent cache kick in
on the very first call (~0ms instead of ~3s).

Running this example a second time will yield a warm cache on both queries, dropping the first call’s time down to fractions of a millisecond.

item.title: Third Party Crates
item.description:
Third Party Crates

Querying methods on types from external crates.

The first time you query a third-party type, Cargo must download and compile the crate inside the ephemeral probe project. This can take 10-30 seconds on a cold cache. Subsequent queries still require Cargo to resolve dependencies inside the ephemeral probe project, so expect similar times on every invocation until persistent probe caching is implemented.

third_party_crate.rs

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::{find_rust_analyzer, query_methods};

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;

    // ── Single external crate ────────────────────────────────────────────────

    let serde_deps = r#"serde_json = "1.0""#;

    println!("Querying serde_json::Value methods (may be slow on first run)...");
    let methods = query_methods("serde_json::Value", &ra_path, Some(serde_deps))?;

    println!("serde_json::Value has {} methods:", methods.len());
    for m in &methods {
        println!("  {}", m.name);
    }

    println!();

    // ── Multiple dependencies ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    //
    // If your type requires more than one crate (e.g. a type that uses serde
    // traits), pass all deps as a single newline-separated string. This maps
    // directly to what Cargo expects under [dependencies].

    let multi_deps = "serde = { version = \"1.0\", features = [\"derive\"] }\nserde_json = \"1.0\"";

    println!("Querying serde_json::Map with serde + serde_json...");
    let map_methods = query_methods(
        "serde_json::Map<String, serde_json::Value>",
        &ra_path,
        Some(multi_deps),
    )?;

    println!("serde_json::Map has {} methods:", map_methods.len());
    for m in &map_methods {
        println!("  {}", m.name);
    }

    Ok(())
}

The same queries using MethodQuery, the .deps() call keeps the dependency string attached to the type it belongs to:

use rust_meth_lib::analyzer::find_rust_analyzer;
use rust_meth_lib::query::MethodQuery;

fn main() -> rust_meth_lib::error::Result<()> {
    let ra_path = find_rust_analyzer()?;

    let methods = MethodQuery::new("serde_json::Value")
        .deps(r#"serde_json = "1.0""#)
        .run(&ra_path)?;

    println!("serde_json::Value has {} methods:", methods.len());
    for m in &methods {
        println!("  {}", m.name);
    }

    println!();

    let map_methods = MethodQuery::new("serde_json::Map<String, serde_json::Value>")
        .deps("serde = { version = \"1.0\", features = [\"derive\"] }\nserde_json = \"1.0\"")
        .run(&ra_path)?;

    println!("serde_json::Map has {} methods:", map_methods.len());
    for m in &map_methods {
        println!("  {}", m.name);
    }

    Ok(())
}
